q: What is Amazon Route 53 primarily used for?

opts.b: Scalable Domain Name System (DNS) web service and domain registration

exp.a: Wrong - That's ELB's role.
exp.b: Correct - Route 53 is AWS's highly available and scalable DNS service that also supports domain registration and health checking.
exp.c: Wrong - That's CloudFront.

q: Why is the AWS DNS service named 'Route 53'?

opts.a: It was the 53rd AWS service launched

exp.a: Wrong - Not related to launch order.
exp.b: Correct - The name 'Route 53' references TCP/UDP port 53, which is the standard port used by DNS.
exp.c: Wrong - Route 53 supports far fewer record types than 53.
exp.d: Wrong - There are far more edge locations.

q: You want to direct users to the AWS region with the LOWEST network latency for them. Which Route 53 routing policy?

exp.a: Wrong - Weighted splits traffic by percentage.
exp.b: Wrong - Geolocation routes based on user's physical location, not measured latency.
exp.c: Correct - Latency-based routing directs users to the AWS region with the lowest measured network latency for them.
exp.d: Wrong - Simple routing has no intelligent selection.

q: What is the default maximum number of hosted zones you can create per AWS account?

exp.a: Wrong - Too low.
exp.b: Correct - The default limit is 500 hosted zones per AWS account (soft limit; can be increased).
exp.c: Wrong - Requires quota increase.

q: What is a Hosted Zone in Route 53?

opts.b: A container for DNS records for a specific domain

exp.a: Wrong - Not a physical concept.
exp.b: Correct - A Hosted Zone is a container that holds information about how you want to route traffic for a domain (e.g., example.com) and its subdomains.
exp.c: Wrong - AZ is unrelated to DNS.

q: What is the difference between a Public Hosted Zone and a Private Hosted Zone in Route 53?

opts.b: Public zones handle internet DNS queries; Private zones resolve DNS only within specified VPCs
opts.d: Public zones are only for AWS services

exp.a: Wrong - They serve different purposes.
exp.b: Correct - Public Hosted Zones respond to DNS queries from the public internet; Private Hosted Zones only respond to queries from within associated VPCs.
exp.c: Wrong - Both have similar pricing.
exp.d: Wrong - Public zones handle any internet-facing DNS.

q: You want to route 80% of traffic to a new app version and 20% to the old for canary testing. Which routing policy?

exp.a: Wrong - Latency doesn't split by percentage.
exp.b: Correct - Weighted routing lets you assign specific traffic percentages (e.g., 80/20) across multiple endpoints, ideal for canary deployments and A/B testing.
exp.c: Wrong - Geolocation splits by user location, not percentage.
exp.d: Wrong - Multi-value returns multiple records but doesn't control percentages.

q: What is a Route 53 Alias record?

opts.b: AWS-specific record that maps a domain to an AWS resource (like ALB, CloudFront, S3) without an IP

exp.a: Wrong - It's more specific than that.
exp.b: Correct - Alias records are AWS-specific, mapping domains to AWS resources (ALB, CloudFront, S3 website, API Gateway, etc.) using the target's DNS name; they're free and support zone apex.
exp.c: Wrong - CNAME doesn't work at zone apex; Alias does.

q: What is the default TTL (Time To Live) for records created in Route 53?

exp.a: Wrong - Too low for default.
exp.b: Correct - The default TTL for Route 53 records is 300 seconds (5 minutes), though it's fully customizable.
exp.c: Wrong - That's 1 hour, not the default.

q: You want traffic routed to a primary region normally, and to a secondary region only if the primary fails. Which routing policy?

exp.a: Wrong - Weighted always splits traffic.
exp.b: Correct - Failover routing with health checks routes traffic to primary; if primary health check fails, it automatically fails over to secondary. Ideal for active-passive DR.
exp.c: Wrong - Latency doesn't do active-passive.
exp.d: Wrong - Multi-value doesn't provide failover behavior.

q: What is the difference between a CNAME record and an Alias record in Route 53?

opts.b: CNAME cannot be used at the zone apex (e.g., example.com); Alias can and is free for AWS resources

exp.a: Wrong - Significant differences exist.
exp.b: Correct - CNAME cannot exist at zone apex (root domain like example.com) per DNS RFC; Alias records can point apex domains to AWS resources and are free of DNS query charges.
exp.c: Wrong - Alias works for many AWS resources (ALB, S3, CloudFront, API Gateway, etc.).

q: You want European users to see content in French from EU servers and US users to see English from US servers. Which routing policy?

exp.a: Wrong - Latency chooses fastest, not by geographic rules.
exp.b: Wrong - Weighted splits by percentage.
exp.c: Correct - Geolocation routing directs traffic based on the geographic location of the DNS query (continent, country, or US state), enabling localization.
exp.d: Wrong - Failover is for DR, not localization.

q: What is the maximum number of records you can have in a single Route 53 hosted zone by default?

exp.a: Wrong - Too low.
exp.b: Wrong - Not the default.
exp.c: Correct - The default limit is 10,000 records per hosted zone (soft limit, can be increased).

q: What is a Route 53 Health Check?

opts.a: A monitoring feature that verifies endpoint availability and can trigger failover routing

exp.a: Correct - Route 53 Health Checks monitor endpoints (via HTTP/HTTPS/TCP), CloudWatch alarms, or calculated health of other checks. Unhealthy targets are excluded from DNS responses.
exp.b: Wrong - Not billing-related.
exp.c: Wrong - It's a separate feature, not a record type.

q: A company has global users but wants all of them to be routed to the closest healthy endpoint. BEST combination?

exp.a: Wrong - Simple has no intelligence.
exp.b: Correct - Latency-based routing sends users to the lowest-latency region; health checks ensure Route 53 only returns healthy endpoints, skipping unhealthy ones.
exp.c: Wrong - Failover is active-passive only.
exp.d: Wrong - Weighted doesn't consider latency or health.

q: What is the maximum number of health checks you can create per AWS account by default in Route 53?

exp.a: Wrong - Too low.
exp.b: Wrong - Not the default.
exp.c: Correct - The default limit is 200 health checks per AWS account (soft limit, can be increased).

q: Which DNS record type maps a domain name to an IPv4 address?

exp.a: Wrong - AAAA is for IPv6.
exp.b: Correct - A (Address) records map a domain name to an IPv4 address (e.g., 192.0.2.1).
exp.c: Wrong - CNAME maps domain to another domain.
exp.d: Wrong - MX is for mail exchange.

q: Which DNS record type maps a domain to an IPv6 address?

exp.a: Wrong - A is for IPv4.
exp.b: Correct - AAAA (Quad-A) records map a domain to an IPv6 address (e.g., 2001:db8::1).
exp.c: Wrong - CNAME maps domain to domain.
exp.d: Wrong - TXT stores text data (e.g., SPF, DKIM).

q: You want a domain example.com to resolve to another domain, say example.otherdomain.com. Which record type?

exp.a: Wrong - A maps to IP, not another domain.
exp.b: Wrong - MX is for mail.
exp.c: Correct - CNAME (Canonical Name) records map one domain name to another. Note: CNAME cannot be used at the zone apex (root domain).

q: What is the purpose of an MX record in DNS?

opts.b: Specifies mail servers for a domain

exp.a: Wrong - That's A records.
exp.b: Correct - MX (Mail Exchange) records specify the mail servers responsible for receiving email for a domain, along with priority values.
exp.c: Wrong - That's TXT.

q: Your Route 53 domain is example.com. You want to point it directly to an S3 static website. What record type should you use?

opts.b: Alias record (A type) pointing to the S3 website endpoint

exp.a: Wrong - CNAME cannot be used at zone apex (example.com).
exp.b: Correct - Use an Alias A record pointing to the S3 static website endpoint. Alias supports zone apex and is free.
exp.c: Wrong - TXT doesn't route traffic.

q: How many DNS query rates does Route 53 support?

exp.a: Wrong - Too low.
exp.b: Wrong - Not the limit.
exp.c: Wrong - Not a hard limit.
exp.d: Correct - Route 53 automatically scales to handle any query volume; there's no fixed query rate limit.

q: What is a TXT record commonly used for?

opts.b: SPF, DKIM, domain verification, and other text-based metadata

exp.a: Wrong - DNS isn't for binary data.
exp.b: Correct - TXT records store text metadata used for SPF/DKIM (email authentication), domain ownership verification, and other services (e.g., for ACM certificate validation).
exp.c: Wrong - That's routing policies.

q: You want to distribute traffic across up to 8 healthy records with basic randomization (no weights or geo logic). Which routing policy?

exp.a: Wrong - Simple returns one record without health checks.
exp.b: Correct - Multi-value answer routing returns up to 8 healthy records randomly, providing basic health-check-based load balancing at the DNS level.
exp.c: Wrong - Weighted requires percentages.

q: What is Route 53 Resolver used for?

opts.b: Enabling DNS resolution between VPCs and on-premises networks (via inbound/outbound endpoints)

exp.a: Wrong - That's DNSSEC.
exp.b: Correct - Route 53 Resolver enables hybrid DNS resolution — inbound endpoints let on-prem resolve AWS DNS; outbound endpoints let AWS resolve on-prem DNS.
exp.c: Wrong - That's Route 53 Registrar.

q: A company's on-premises DNS server needs to resolve names for AWS private hosted zones. BEST solution?

exp.a: Wrong - Private zones aren't publicly resolvable.
exp.b: Correct - Route 53 Resolver Inbound Endpoints provide IPs that on-premises DNS servers can forward queries to, resolving AWS private zone records.
exp.c: Wrong - CloudFront is CDN, not DNS.
exp.d: Wrong - VPC peering handles network, not DNS resolution.

q: What is DNSSEC in Route 53?

opts.b: DNS Security Extensions that add cryptographic signatures to DNS responses to prevent spoofing

exp.a: Wrong - That's CloudFront.
exp.b: Correct - DNSSEC (DNS Security Extensions) authenticates DNS responses with cryptographic signatures, preventing DNS spoofing and cache poisoning attacks. Route 53 supports DNSSEC signing.
exp.c: Wrong - Not a backup mechanism.

q: You want to register a new domain name (e.g., mycompany.com) via AWS. Which service?

exp.a: Wrong - ACM issues SSL/TLS certificates.
exp.b: Correct - Route 53 acts as an ICANN-accredited domain registrar, allowing you to purchase and manage domain registrations directly.
exp.c: Wrong - CloudFormation is IaC.

q: What is the minimum TTL value you can configure for a Route 53 record?

exp.a: Correct - The minimum TTL for Route 53 records is 0 seconds (though 0 is rarely practical; low values increase query load).
exp.b: Wrong - Minimum is 0.
exp.c: Wrong - Common but not the minimum.

q: What is the purpose of a Route 53 Traffic Policy?

opts.b: Visual editor to create complex routing configurations combining multiple policies (geo, weighted, failover)

exp.a: Wrong - Not billing.
exp.b: Correct - Traffic Policies provide a visual editor to build complex DNS routing configurations combining multiple routing policies (weighted, latency, geolocation, failover) in a single tree.
exp.c: Wrong - DNSSEC is separate.

q: You want to fail over to a backup site when your primary is unhealthy, and use latency-based routing among healthy regions. What can you use?

opts.b: Traffic Policy combining Failover + Latency-based routing

exp.a: Wrong - Failover alone doesn't handle multi-region latency.
exp.b: Correct - Route 53 Traffic Policies let you combine multiple routing policies (e.g., Failover on top of Latency-based) into a decision tree for complex scenarios.
exp.c: Wrong - Simple doesn't support multi-policy logic.
exp.d: Wrong - CNAME chaining is unreliable and not scalable.

q: What is a Route 53 Health Check 'calculated health check'?

opts.b: A health check that combines the status of multiple other health checks using boolean logic (AND/OR/NOT)

exp.a: Wrong - Not billing-related.
exp.b: Correct - Calculated health checks aggregate the status of multiple child health checks with logical operators, useful for complex health decisions.
exp.c: Wrong - Not a DNS record.
exp.d: Wrong - It uses CloudWatch integration but isn't itself a metric.

q: You want Route 53 to monitor a metric in CloudWatch (e.g., queue depth) and trigger DNS failover based on it. Which health check type?

exp.a: Wrong - HTTP checks only pings a URL.
exp.b: Wrong - TCP checks connectivity only.
exp.c: Correct - CloudWatch alarm health checks monitor any CloudWatch metric (like SQS queue depth, custom application metrics) and mark health based on the alarm state.
exp.d: Wrong - Calculated combines other health checks, not metrics directly.

q: How often does Route 53 evaluate a standard health check by default?

exp.a: Wrong - That's the fast interval (extra cost).
exp.b: Correct - Standard Route 53 health checks run every 30 seconds by default. Fast checks (every 10 seconds) are available at additional cost.
exp.c: Wrong - Not the standard interval.

q: In Route 53, what is the SOA record?

opts.b: Start of Authority record that contains administrative information about a DNS zone

exp.a: Wrong - Not a security concept.
exp.b: Correct - SOA (Start of Authority) records store administrative info about a DNS zone including the primary name server, admin email, serial number, and refresh timers.
exp.c: Wrong - Not an AWS-specific term.
exp.d: Wrong - Not a valid DNS record.

q: What is an NS record in Route 53?

opts.b: Name Server record that identifies authoritative DNS servers for a domain

exp.a: Wrong - Not a valid term.
exp.b: Correct - NS (Name Server) records identify the authoritative name servers for a domain. Route 53 creates these automatically when a hosted zone is created.
exp.c: Wrong - Not a real DNS type.

q: You created a hosted zone for example.com in Route 53 but the domain doesn't resolve. Most likely cause?

opts.a: You didn't create an A record
opts.b: You didn't update the domain registrar's NS records to point to Route 53's name servers

exp.a: Wrong - Missing A records only affects specific subdomains.
exp.b: Correct - After creating a hosted zone in Route 53, you must update your domain registrar to use the 4 name servers Route 53 provides, or DNS queries won't reach Route 53.
exp.c: Wrong - TTL affects caching, not resolution failure.
exp.d: Wrong - AWS outages are rare and this is user misconfiguration.

q: How many name servers does Route 53 assign to each hosted zone by default?

exp.a: Wrong - Too few for redundancy.
exp.b: Wrong - Not the Route 53 count.
exp.c: Correct - Route 53 assigns 4 name servers per hosted zone (in different AWS locations) for redundancy and fault tolerance.

q: What does the PTR record do in DNS?

opts.a: Maps an IP to a domain (reverse DNS lookup)
opts.b: Maps a domain to an IP

exp.a: Correct - PTR (Pointer) records perform reverse DNS lookups, mapping an IP address back to a domain name — commonly used for email server verification.
exp.b: Wrong - That's A/AAAA.
exp.c: Wrong - That's MX.

q: You need to route traffic based on the source IP address of the DNS resolver (approximate user location). Which routing policy?

exp.a: Wrong - Not a standard Route 53 policy name.
exp.b: Wrong - Geolocation uses continent/country mapping, not IP proximity.
exp.c: Correct - Geoproximity routing uses the physical distance between user and resource, and you can shift traffic using a 'bias' value. Requires Route 53 Traffic Flow.
exp.d: Wrong - Weighted uses percentages, not location.

q: What is the difference between Geolocation and Geoproximity routing policies?

opts.a: Geolocation uses user's geographic location (country/continent); Geoproximity uses distance from resource with adjustable bias
opts.c: Geoproximity is free; Geolocation is paid
opts.d: Geolocation is only for AWS regions

exp.a: Correct - Geolocation routes based on user's country/continent/state; Geoproximity routes based on physical distance and allows biasing traffic toward or away from specific resources.
exp.b: Wrong - They differ significantly.
exp.c: Wrong - Both have similar pricing model.

q: Your primary us-east-1 endpoint is unhealthy. Route 53 failover is configured. What happens next?

opts.a: Route 53 returns the primary endpoint anyway
opts.b: Route 53 automatically returns the secondary endpoint until primary becomes healthy

exp.a: Wrong - Failover excludes unhealthy primary.
exp.b: Correct - When primary fails its health check, Route 53 automatically returns the secondary endpoint. Once primary is healthy again, traffic returns to it (based on TTL caching).
exp.c: Wrong - Failover prevents that.

q: What is the maximum number of records that Multi-Value Answer routing can return in a single response?

exp.a: Wrong - Too few.
exp.b: Wrong - Not the max.
exp.c: Correct - Multi-Value Answer routing returns up to 8 healthy records randomly in a single DNS response, providing simple DNS-based load balancing.

q: Which record type is used to prove domain ownership for issuing an ACM SSL certificate?

exp.a: Wrong - A records don't validate ownership.
exp.b: Correct - AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) DNS validation requires you to create a specific CNAME record in Route 53 proving control of the domain. Route 53 can auto-add these for you.
exp.c: Wrong - MX is for mail servers.

q: You want to control which VPCs can resolve records in your private hosted zone. What must you do?

opts.b: Explicitly associate the specific VPCs with the private hosted zone

exp.a: Wrong - That defeats the purpose of private.
exp.b: Correct - A private hosted zone only resolves for VPCs explicitly associated with it. You must associate each VPC (same or cross-account) that needs to resolve records.
exp.c: Wrong - VPC peering alone doesn't share private zones.
exp.d: Wrong - NACLs don't affect DNS scoping.

q: What is the primary benefit of using Alias records over CNAME for AWS resources?

opts.a: Alias records support the zone apex and are free (no DNS query charges)
opts.b: Alias records are faster than CNAME
opts.c: Alias records support wildcards; CNAME doesn't

exp.a: Correct - Alias records work at the zone apex (unlike CNAME), don't incur DNS query charges when pointing to AWS resources, and automatically update if the target's IP changes.
exp.b: Wrong - Performance is comparable.
exp.c: Wrong - Both support wildcards.

q: A company wants their domain example.com (zone apex) to point to a CloudFront distribution. Which record type must they use?

exp.a: Wrong - CNAME is not allowed at the zone apex per DNS RFC.
exp.b: Correct - Only Alias records (A type) can point the zone apex (example.com) to AWS resources like CloudFront distributions.
exp.c: Wrong - TXT doesn't route traffic.
exp.d: Wrong - MX is for mail routing.

q: What is the additional cost for a Route 53 fast health check (10-second interval) compared to standard (30-second)?

opts.b: Slightly higher per-month fee per health check

exp.a: Wrong - Not free.
exp.b: Correct - Fast health checks (10-second interval) cost slightly more per month than standard 30-second checks. Also HTTPS and string-matching options incur small extra fees.
exp.c: Wrong - Not that expensive.

q: What is a 'sloppy' vs 'strict' health check pass in Route 53?

opts.a: Sloppy allows some failures; strict requires all endpoints healthy
opts.b: Not real Route 53 terms; health checks use a failure threshold (default 3 consecutive failures) before marking unhealthy

exp.a: Wrong - Not accurate terminology.
exp.b: Correct - Route 53 uses a failure threshold — by default, 3 consecutive failed checks are required before marking an endpoint unhealthy, avoiding false positives.
exp.c: Wrong - Not a real term.

q: You want to prevent DNS resolution for certain domains (blocklist) within your VPC. BEST solution?

exp.a: Correct - Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall lets you filter outbound DNS queries from your VPC, blocking or allowing specific domains via managed or custom domain lists.
exp.b: Wrong - SGs work on ports/IPs, not domains.
exp.c: Wrong - Doesn't block external DNS lookups.
exp.d: Wrong - NACLs work on IPs, not domain names.

q: What is the purpose of Route 53 Resolver Query Logging?

opts.a: Log DNS queries from resources in your VPCs for security auditing and troubleshooting

exp.a: Correct - Route 53 Resolver Query Logging captures information about DNS queries made from within your VPCs, useful for security analysis, threat detection, and troubleshooting.
exp.b: Wrong - Not billing-related.
exp.c: Wrong - That's ACM.

q: You want geolocation routing but need a default answer for users whose location doesn't match any geolocation rule. What should you configure?

opts.a: It's impossible; queries fail without a match
opts.b: Create a Default geolocation record as fallback

exp.a: Wrong - Default records handle this case.
exp.b: Correct - When using Geolocation routing, you should create a 'Default' record that answers queries from locations not covered by specific geolocation rules, preventing NXDOMAIN.
exp.c: Wrong - Failover is a different pattern.
exp.d: Wrong - Weighted doesn't handle geographic fallback.

q: What is the cost of a Route 53 hosted zone per month (base charge)?

exp.a: Wrong - Not the correct rate.
exp.b: Correct - A Route 53 hosted zone costs $0.50 per month for the first 25 zones, then $0.10 per zone thereafter. DNS queries and health checks are charged separately.
exp.c: Wrong - Not the base charge.

q: Which of these is NOT a valid Route 53 routing policy?

exp.a: Wrong - Weighted is valid.
exp.b: Wrong - Latency-based is valid.
exp.c: Correct - 'Bandwidth-based' is NOT a Route 53 routing policy. Valid ones are: Simple, Weighted, Latency, Failover, Geolocation, Geoproximity, Multi-Value Answer, and IP-based.

q: You have a private hosted zone in Account A that VPCs in Account B need to resolve. BEST approach?

opts.b: Use cross-account VPC association: Account A authorizes association from Account B
opts.c: Copy the zone to Account B

exp.a: Wrong - Cross-account is supported.
exp.b: Correct - Route 53 supports cross-account private hosted zone associations: Account A creates authorization for Account B's VPC ID, then Account B associates its VPC.
exp.c: Wrong - Copying creates duplicate management overhead.
exp.d: Wrong - Defeats the purpose of private.

q: What does Route 53 return for a DNS query when ALL endpoints in a Multi-Value Answer policy are unhealthy?

exp.a: Wrong - Not NXDOMAIN.
exp.b: Correct - If all records are unhealthy, Route 53 returns all values (treated as healthy) as a last-resort fallback to avoid total service unavailability.
exp.c: Wrong - Empty responses aren't returned.

q: A domain registered outside AWS needs to use Route 53 for DNS. What must you do?

opts.a: Transfer the domain to Route 53 registrar
opts.b: At the current registrar, update the name servers (NS) to point to the 4 Route 53 name servers listed in your hosted zone

exp.a: Wrong - Transfer isn't required to use Route 53 DNS.
exp.b: Correct - You can keep the domain registered elsewhere but delegate DNS to Route 53 by updating the NS records at your current registrar to Route 53's 4 name servers.
exp.c: Wrong - Delegation must be explicitly configured.

q: For how long can a domain registered via Route 53 be renewed at once?

exp.a: Wrong - Not fixed to 1 year.
exp.b: Correct - Route 53 supports domain registration/renewal from 1 to 10 years at a time, depending on TLD rules (e.g., .com allows up to 10 years).
exp.c: Wrong - Depends on TLD, not a fixed 5.
exp.d: Wrong - Domains must be renewed periodically.

q: Which DNS record helps prevent email spoofing by specifying authorized sender IPs?

exp.a: Wrong - MX defines mail servers but doesn't authenticate senders.
exp.b: Correct - SPF (Sender Policy Framework) records are stored in TXT records and specify which IPs are authorized to send email on behalf of the domain, preventing spoofing.
exp.c: Wrong - AAAA is for IPv6.

q: You want CloudWatch metrics on the health status of your Route 53 endpoints. What should you enable?

opts.b: Health checks with CloudWatch metrics enabled

exp.a: Wrong - Health checks aren't automatically created.
exp.b: Correct - Route 53 Health Checks emit CloudWatch metrics (like HealthCheckStatus, HealthCheckPercentHealthy) that you can monitor and alarm on.
exp.c: Wrong - Flow Logs are for VPC traffic.

q: What is the maximum number of IP addresses a Route 53 health check can monitor for a single endpoint?

exp.a: Correct - Each Route 53 health check monitors 1 endpoint (IP or domain name). To monitor multiple endpoints, create multiple health checks and optionally combine them using calculated health checks.
exp.b: Wrong - Not the design.
exp.c: Wrong - One health check = one endpoint.

q: You want to send email from your domain via SES. Which Route 53 records must you configure?

opts.b: MX record (optional, for receiving), TXT records for SPF/DKIM/DMARC verification

exp.a: Wrong - A alone doesn't enable email.
exp.b: Correct - For SES: configure MX (if receiving), TXT for SPF, CNAME/TXT for DKIM verification, and TXT for DMARC policy. This authenticates outbound mail and enables deliverability.
exp.c: Wrong - NS delegates DNS, doesn't set up email.
exp.d: Wrong - PTR is set by IP owner, not domain owner.
